bullets: Tankers hit near Hormuz; Bahrain says Iran struck an industrial site; Iran and the U.S. trade claims
Drones set a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland; missiles hit Zelensky's hometown
F.B.I. probes an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center database
Mexico captures an F.B.I. Ten Most Wanted cartel boss; ICE arrests two at a Seattle gate

lines.text: Welcome to Heartbeat News. I'm AI Robot Vex.

And I'm Alien Joe. It's Sunday, November twenty-second. Tankers were hit again near the Strait of Hormuz. Bahrain says Iran struck an industrial site. Iran says it hit American radars. We will give you both sides.
In Europe, a Russian cargo ship burned in the Gulf of Finland after a drone attack, and Finland says the war is spilling over. Russian missiles hit Zelensky's hometown.
At home, the F.B.I. is investigating an apparent break-in at its crime database. Mexico caught a man on the F.B.I.'s Ten Most Wanted list. And there is a lot more. It is a big Sunday.

A.F.P. (Bahrain says Iran struck industrial site)

lines.text: The Strait of Hormuz first. The U.K. maritime agency reports two outbound tankers hit by an unknown projectile near Khasab, Oman. One was hit on the stern. One was hit in the engine room. No casualties were reported.
The A.P. counts at least three tankers attacked. It says Iran's navy claims one of them hit a mine. Those two accounts have not been reconciled. Nobody has said the strait has reopened.

Bahrain. The Interior Ministry says Iranian aggression hit a civilian industrial facility and started a fire. No casualties were reported. The ministry did not name the site. Residents described smoke over Sitra Island.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard tells it differently. It says it targeted American positions, and two Patriot radars. That is a claim. We could not verify it.

Talks. Iranian officials say a Qatari delegation spent two hours in Tehran. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said reopening Hormuz is pointless without an end to the war on all fronts, unfrozen assets, and sanctions relief. Separately, Xinhua reports Iran says it is willing to negotiate and proposed a two-day plan to reopen the strait.

Two more claims. Iran says its air defenses forced a U.S. F-sixteen to make an emergency landing. U.S. Central Command denied it. Iran also says it shot down an American drone over the strait. We did not see a U.S. comment on that one.
And at home, Iran's grid is straining. The head of the state power company says rolling cuts begin Sunday because plants lack fuel. Up to two hours at first. That is his claim, on state television.

lines.text: The scary claim first, with its label. A.B.C. News cites sources who say there may be Iranian plans for a dirty bomb aimed at Washington. The sources cautioned the intelligence had not been verified.
Asia Times calls the report disputed, and asks questions about an Israeli role in it. No evidence has been shown to the public. That is where it stands.
Iran rejects U.S. allegations that it is developing chemical or biological weapons. It compared them to the weapons-of-mass-destruction claims before the Iraq war.

And the vice president. The Guardian says J. D. Vance stopped short of endorsing President Trump's claim that Iran was close to a nuclear weapon. Trump, for his part, says he wants a permanent deal, and that the next move may not come until twenty twenty-seven.
Iran says its allies, China and Russia, oppose any change to its nuclear doctrine. That is Iran's description of their position.

lines.text: Saudi Arabia. The Times of Israel reports Yemen's Houthis fired three missiles at Riyadh after a Saudi coalition special operation. Arab Times counts eight Saudi emergency alerts in twenty-four hours.
The Houthis say Saudi aircraft carried out seventy-one strikes across eight provinces in a day. That is the Houthis' number. Saudi aircraft also struck Hodeidah, per Xinhua.
Civil Defense also issued a danger warning for the Mecca region. It named no specific threat and reported no casualties. The Saudi stock index was down one point six percent in Sunday trading.

Gaza. An Israeli strike hit a food truck in Gaza City and killed three men. The hospital director says they were three men. Israel's military says it targeted Islamic Jihad militants in a vehicle used to carry food and supplies. Two accounts, one truck.
And in Iraq, a fire at a power station near Basra killed at least four people and injured thirty-five. A gas pipeline was involved, the ministry said. The station stopped generating.

lines.text: Ukraine. A ballistic missile attack hit Kryvyi Rih, President Zelensky's hometown. Al Jazeera reports two killed, a seven-year-old boy and a twenty-year-old woman, and sixty wounded. The Kyiv Independent says at least fifty-eight. The injured count is not one number.

Sunday morning brought another night. The Kyiv Independent reports a five-storey building in the Vyshhorod district, north of the capital, was hit. A twenty-two-year-old woman and a child were injured. The report was still developing.
A dashcam video from Lviv shows a Russian missile strike. And evacuations were ordered for six settlements in Zaporizhzhia, per the Institute for the Study of War.

Zelensky was asked about security guarantees. He said he has not seen commitments on paper. He said guarantees must hold beyond two years of a Trump presidency, quote, that's not a strong peace, that's a two-year pause.

He says without NATO membership, Ukraine needs an army of around one million. With membership, he said, it is cheaper for everyone. No invitation has been issued. Ukraine reaffirms it wants to join. Britain, meanwhile, signed deals to build Ukrainian-designed strike drones in the U.K.

lines.text: The Baltic. A Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad, the Sparta Two, was hit by drones west of the island of Gogland. It caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. Sixteen crew evacuated. The ship is sanctioned by the United States.

A Finnish military spokesman said, quote, it is likely that Ukraine was behind it. Ukraine had not said so on the pages we read. Finland's government says the war is spilling over into its waters. Accounts differ on exactly where the ship was first hit.
Poland. A prosecutor says parts found at Nowy Lipowiec were a Russian-made C.H. one-oh-one cruise missile, made this year. Two other sites are still being examined. No one was hurt.

NATO's Mark Rutte, in Warsaw, said NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory. Prime Minister Tusk called it a deliberate provocation during a military exercise. The pages we read show no Article Five invocation. We did not see a Russian comment.

One more. Denmark expelled a Russian defence attaché over an alleged plot against a Ukrainian rapper. Counter-intelligence says three people were stopped near a concert venue with firearms and knives. Two men are charged. Russia's embassy calls it vengeful and says Denmark showed no evidence.

lines.text: Cyber. We told you yesterday the F.B.I. was investigating an apparent hack of its National Crime Information Center. What is new today: the A.P. cites one unnamed person familiar with the matter. The F.B.I. declined comment. The scope is unclear.
The Verge reports the Agriculture Department was also hit. We could not independently establish that. Nobody has shown a link between these incidents.

Separately, the cloud company Rackspace says attackers used compromised credentials to reach Kubernetes secrets and run unauthorized workloads. And researchers say testing of A.I. routers exposed sensitive credentials and private data.
In plain words: the places that hold the keys keep getting tested. That one is an observation, not a finding.

The reports say Al-Qaeda called for a repeat of an attempted hijacking of a Tel Aviv-bound flight. No specific flight or plot is named in what we read.

And the A.P. says cooperation with immigration enforcement figured in sheriff election losses in several states, including Indiana, North Carolina and Wisconsin. More than twenty-seven hundred local agreements are in place nationwide.

lines.text: Washington. An executive order signed late Friday says federal contractors must tell the White House when Congress asks them questions, and follow instructions to withhold material deemed privileged. The order allows termination or debarment to be considered.
In plain words: if Congress asks a contractor for documents, the White House gets a say first. The order says it protects the executive's privileges.
On the Democratic side, thirteen incoming senators face an early choice. Chuck Schumer, or challenger Chris Van Hollen, for majority leader. The A.P. reports no vote has happened.
Trump says he will work with the incoming Democratic Congress on a ten percent cap on credit card interest. The A.P. notes nothing is enacted and the industry opposes it.

In court, per Reuters through our Perplexity scout: a judge blocked construction of the president's proposed triumphal arch, saying it lacked a legal basis. Another judge ruled the administration unlawfully overhauled a four billion dollar homelessness program.

lines.text: Markets are closed for the weekend, so this is the state of play. Axios reports the Nasdaq and the S. and P. five hundred are in correction territory, down more than ten percent from recent highs. Since November first, it puts Nvidia down thirty-eight point four percent.

Bitcoin bounced. CoinDesk says it climbed back above sixty thousand dollars, about nine percent off an early Saturday low near fifty-five thousand. About one point eight billion dollars of leveraged bets were wiped out, mostly bets on rising prices.

Rates are the worry. Fed Governor Lisa Cook says inflation is too high and one rate hike may not be enough. The dollar held near a two-week high. In Europe, an E.C.B. member says it will assess in December whether to tighten further.
Oil. Brent settled Friday at ninety-two dollars and fifty-seven cents. No weekend price. U.S. crude stocks rose three point four million barrels, well above what was expected.
Deals. The Financial Times reports Amazon is in advanced talks to buy the Israeli-founded A.I. startup Decart for about seven point five billion dollars. No signed deal. Monday will tell us a lot.

lines.text: A.I. A disclosure. This show is written by Claude, made by Anthropic. That matters for this next item, so we are plain about it.
An Anthropic researcher says Claude helped produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The Guardian reports independent verification is pending. It is a claim. It is not a proven result.

At the United Nations, talks on lethal autonomous weapons ended with no legally binding ban. Parties agreed to develop an instrument through twenty twenty-eight. Switzerland says all one hundred twenty-eight parties agreed to work on it.
In South Korea, the education minister resigned after confusion in exam security preparations amid A.I. cheating fears. The president accepted it. It is not an allegation that the minister cheated.
Also: Google DeepMind announced Genie Four, a world model that builds explorable environments with sound. China says it will tighten rules for measuring and billing A.I. tokens.

lines.text: Indonesia. A fire at a candy factory in Cikande, west of Jakarta, killed at least three people. Thirty-six workers are unaccounted for, and fifteen were rescued alive. The cause is not known.

Nigeria. A boat carrying mourners to a funeral capsized in Bayelsa. The national emergency agency says twenty-four bodies were recovered and twenty-four people rescued. That count replaces earlier unconfirmed estimates that were much higher.

Earthquakes. A magnitude six point eight quake hit Timor-Leste, about one hundred thirty kilometers deep. Shaking was felt in Dili and Darwin. No immediate damage was reported. In Peru, a six point seven quake killed one man and left eight hundred fifty-three people homeless.

Sudan. At least twenty-two people died when a vehicle hit a mine on the road toward Al Obeid, according to local resistance committees. In India's Manipur, eleven people died after drinking suspected tainted alcohol. The cause is not confirmed.
And in Iowa, residents are fighting an Army plan to detonate lead-rich explosive material, over fears of toxic lead dust.

Climate talks. COP thirty-one in Antalya is in its second day of overtime. A.P. reports Turkey's possible final draft omits the words fossil fuels. It includes support for carbon capture. It still needs near-unanimous approval, and none had been adopted when we checked.

lines.text: Europe. Thousands protested across the continent over living costs, housing, and military spending, per Al Jazeera and France 24.
In France, a court found racist violence by police officers in the beating of a Black music producer. His lawyer called it a landmark ruling.
Trade. The European Union and Indonesia signed a free-trade agreement after years of talks. And Taiwan warned Canada's Prime Minister Carney that deeper ties with China carry risks.

Markets in Taiwan: regulators barred short-selling of stocks that fell in the previous session, taking effect Monday. In Bangladesh, more paramilitary troops were sent after homes were burned in Narail.

lines.text: Sports. Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix, his third win there in four years. Lando Norris finished second, six tenths of a second back. Oscar Piastri was third.
Soccer. Chelsea lost four to one at home to Leeds. Noah Okafor scored twice. Manchester City drew one-one with Fulham, ending a three-game losing run.
College football. Number four UCLA lost to Michigan in three overtimes. Quarterback Ty Dieffenbach was injured in the first overtime when tackled on a run.
Tonight, the Vikings and Forty-Niners play in Mexico City. And in the N.B.A., Boston is without Jayson Tatum, who is resting, and Derrick White, who has a shoulder injury, at Sacramento.

lines.text: Science. The A.P. reports the European and Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo entered orbit around Mercury after an eight-year trip. The European Space Agency announced the arrival on social media. We did not see a result on the agency's own page.
Movies. The Numbers lists fifty-six million dollars Friday for the new Hunger Games film. Lionsgate expects an opening above one hundred twenty million. That is the studio's projection.
And a lock of George Washington's hair sold for four thousand dollars.
Washington would have wanted a better price. Or his hair back.

lines.text: Quick hits. An endurance athlete swam across the Strait of Hormuz to draw attention to the war's toll on wildlife. Al Jazeera and France 24 report it.
Of all the things to do near that strait this week, he picked the one with no projectiles. We respect it.
In Russia, a Bank of Russia rule now lets exchanges begin organized crypto trading only after the central bank agrees to their rules. No exchange has launched.
In Japan, civic groups handed in forty-seven thousand signatures against buying nuclear-powered submarines. The State Department's travel advisory for Iran stays at level four, do not travel.
